who: Adult siblings who share hands-on care of an elderly parent and each administer some of the daily medication doses
what_breaks: Medication apps log that a dose was taken but not which family member gave it, so siblings re-ask each other in the family group chat and risk double-dosing.
quote: it is difficult to track exactly who administered a dose. We often face confusion or duplicate questions in our family chats.
volume_evidence: Medisafe has ~101,000 US App Store ratings; in a sample of the 250 most recent US reviews, 7 explicitly describe multi-family-member caregiving use of the shared 'Medfriends' feature.
workaround: Family group chat used as the audit trail — siblings text each other to confirm each dose was given.

who: Adult children who take over a parent's finances under POA while a sibling holds medical POA
what_breaks: There is no shared system for the money side of caregiving, so the financial-POA sibling rebuilds an expense ledger in Excel from scratch every month.
quote: I used excel spreadsheet sheets to track monthly expenses (paying caregivers, tracking mileage, groceries, medications, personal needs, etc). One of my sisters was financial POA and I was MPOA.
volume_evidence: Thread drew 14 separate answers within days on AgingCare's caregiver forum; nearly every respondent named a manual system (Excel, Google Sheets, three-ring binders, composition books, manila folders).
workaround: Excel spreadsheets for monthly expenses, mileage and caregiver payments, split by POA role between siblings.

who: Adult children newly managing a parent's care who must document every dollar in case of a future Medicaid application
what_breaks: No consumer tool handles paying a parent's bills, categorizing costs, and reimbursing siblings while producing documentation that survives a Medicaid lookback.
quote: I am paying bills, tracking costs by category plus reimbursing family members for purchases they make on her behalf. Need good documentation for Medicaid if needed in future.
volume_evidence: 7 answers on AgingCare; the accepted approaches were all manual (spiral binder, ledger paper and manila envelopes, Excel), and a later replier confirmed organized spreadsheets 'put us WAY ahead of the game' with Illinois Medicaid.
workaround: A spiral binder: "I'm no accountant, so I just used a spiral binder and wrote down everything. I'd write the amount, what it was for, and the check number and I kept the receipts in an envelope."

who: Divorced parents under a court-ordered co-parenting app whose expense agreement is not a 50/50 split
what_breaks: The expense module only supports fixed preset split categories, so a parent with a 70/30 or per-item agreement cannot record what is actually owed and the ledger shows $0.00.
quote: Not everyone fits into 50/50 scenarios of splitting expenses and there is no way to enter custom %
volume_evidence: OurFamilyWizard has ~53,500 US ratings; across 800 sampled reviews of OurFamilyWizard, AppClose and TalkingParents, 185 mention screenshots, exports, printing or court, i.e. using the app as an evidence ledger.
workaround: Side agreements tracked outside the app; parents screenshot and print message threads to bring to court.

who: Parents in high-conflict custody arrangements who need a defensible daily record of a child's routine
what_breaks: Court-mandated co-parenting apps log messages and calendars but have no structured daily log, so parents free-type observations into calendar notes that don't export as a record.
quote: It would make high conflict co-parenting much easier to have the extra data all in the same place.
volume_evidence: AppClose has ~39,000 US ratings; 76 of 250 sampled recent reviews reference screenshots, exports, printing or court use. A 2016 reviewer of a rival app concluded: "create a spreadsheet and call it a day, that's my plan..."
workaround: Typing school times, meals, sleep, medications and behavior into calendar notes, then exporting chat reports; others keep spreadsheets.

who: Newly diagnosed celiac adults who need to know about shared-equipment cross-contact, not just what's printed on the label
what_breaks: Food-scanning apps only parse the declared ingredient list, so the user still has to google each product or phone the manufacturer about cross-contamination.
quote: If I still have to google whether something is celiac safe or if I have to contact the company, your app is useless to my dietary restriction.
volume_evidence: Fig has ~16,200 US ratings; 35 of 400 sampled recent reviews mention celiac, gluten or cross-contamination specifically.
workaround: Googling each product individually in the grocery aisle and emailing or calling manufacturers to ask about shared lines.

who: Two-parent households co-tracking a newborn's feeds and sleep in the first months
what_breaks: Baby trackers are built around a single account, so partners either share one login or each keep partial logs that never merge.
quote: it’s been so easy for me and my partner to use with our newborn i wish it would have two people share a account
volume_evidence: Huckleberry has ~73,100 US ratings; 13 of 150 sampled recent reviews reference a partner, spouse or the need for two people on one account.
workaround: Sharing one login between both parents, or one parent logging everything and relaying by text.

who: Families coordinating visitors and updates for a relative in extended hospital or hospice care
what_breaks: Illness-update platforms broadcast journal posts but have no shared visit calendar, so the family coordinates who is visiting when over text.
quote: I wish there was a way to share a calendar so that planning visits would be shared.
volume_evidence: CaringBridge has ~19,500 US ratings; 9 of the 100 sampled recent reviews raise calendar or visit-coordination needs.
workaround: Group texts and phone calls to stagger who visits on which day; separate shared calendars maintained by hand.

who: Teenagers in school activity groups whose parents run contact-approval parental monitoring
what_breaks: Every unknown number in an activity group chat has to be individually approved by a parent, so the teen is effectively locked out of logistics threads for band, sports and rehearsals.
quote: I have to manually request contacts, which made being on group chats horrendous. I had to literally sort through numbers and pray that it was the correct person
volume_evidence: Bark has ~35,600 US ratings at 4.25 avg; 38 of 500 sampled recent reviews describe manual approval, syncing or contact-management burden.
workaround: Teen manually requests each contact and explains each person to a parent; parents fall back to physically checking the phone.

who: School administrators and teachers in districts with large Spanish-speaking parent populations
what_breaks: The parent-communication platform delivers inbound parent messages in the parent's language with no inbound translation, so staff paste each message into Google Translate to read it.
quote: I also have a few parents who message me in Spanish, which I’m not able to read & have to use Google translate to read their message
volume_evidence: Remind has ~1.79M US ratings. A second teacher review (2026-03-09) independently asks for the same thing: "I also wish Remind translated for parents who don’t speak English." TalkingPoints' entire review base is ESL/ESOL teachers who switched for exactly this.
workaround: Copy-pasting inbound parent messages into Google Translate; asking another teacher or a student to translate for parents.

who: Self-directed adult learners of highly inflected languages (Hungarian, Slavic, Finnish) building their own conjugation drills
what_breaks: Conjugation reference sites publish HTML tables but no export, so learners hand-copy tables into spreadsheets and reshape them into flashcards one verb at a time.
quote: I am copying and pasting verb conjugation tables into a spreadsheet and then spending hours editing the spreadsheet for just a handful of verbs.
volume_evidence: 589 views on the Anki forum thread with no working answer; the WaniKani community has parallel user-built threads publishing hand-made .xlsx conjugation spreadsheets for Japanese verbs and adjectives.
workaround: Copy-pasting conjugator site tables into Excel and manually editing them into card fields; considering paying someone to do the data entry.

who: Older, non-technical adults learning a language who already have a vocabulary list in Excel
what_breaks: The dominant spaced-repetition tool requires understanding decks, subdecks, sibling burying and scheduling before it will turn a two-column spreadsheet into flashcards.
quote: Is there not some straightforward software which enables one to produce randomised flashcards from an Excel spreadsheet vocabulary list?
volume_evidence: 4,185 views and 13 replies on the Anki forum; the thread's eventual answers were a ChatGPT-generated CSV walkthrough and a suggestion to use paper Leitner boxes.
workaround: Giving up and using a physical Leitner box of index cards, or pasting the spreadsheet into ChatGPT for CSV conversion instructions.

who: K-12 teachers who built their class study sets on Quizlet and lost the Learn mode to the paywall
what_breaks: Teachers have years of sets in spreadsheet form and no simple path to bulk-import them into a free study tool mid-semester.
quote: I’m a teacher in a crunch since Quizlet just put their “learn” feature behind a pay wall.
volume_evidence: 6,699 views on this single migration thread. Quizlet's own recent App Store reviews confirm the trigger: "you get one test option for each set, after that it is a locked option. While you cannot use the 'learn' feature without a subscription." (2026-09-09)
workaround: Exporting sets to CSV and hand-importing into Anki with community help.

who: Parents of high school juniors and seniors comparing colleges on cost, admit rate and program fit
what_breaks: Common Data Set figures are published per-school as static files, so parents retype them college by college into their own Google Sheet to run any custom filter.
quote: you have to gather and input all of the data yourself, which is so dumb considering the point of the Common Data Set is that the data is in a structured format
volume_evidence: Four separate parents in an 8-post thread each described building their own spreadsheet; one noted parents 'circulate their own spreadsheets among friends or on Facebook'. College Confidential's class-year parent threads run to thousands of posts with recurring spreadsheet-sharing requests.
workaround: Hand-built Google Sheets with raw CDS columns plus derived columns (admit %, draw rate), rebuilt each application year and passed between friends.

who: Parents of elementary students whose school pushes all logistics through a classroom messaging app
what_breaks: Field trip forms, deadlines and permission details arrive as an unsearchable chronological feed, so the detail you need the night before is unrecoverable.
quote: I wish there was a search bar to find key words- like being able to find the field trip information that came out a month ago when the field trip is tomorrow.
volume_evidence: ClassDojo has ~4.05M US ratings; 11 of 500 sampled recent reviews raise search/scrolling/findability. A ParentSquare reviewer (2026-08-20) makes the same complaint: "There is no way to distinguish if it is just a regular update or an important message."
workaround: Scrolling back through weeks of feed; Seesaw parents ask for a photo folder because "teachers upload pictures of papers containing crucial information" that then can't be found.

who: Parents who receive their child's paper permission slips and handouts as photos posted inside a classroom app
what_breaks: Photographed documents are buried in a message stream with no folder or document view, so parents re-scroll months of messages to find a form.
quote: Many teachers upload pictures of papers containing crucial information, and it becomes quite tedious to search through past messages to locate them.
volume_evidence: Seesaw has ~100,000 US ratings; a parallel review asks for "folders or search engine that locates documents" so "parents could use as much help as possible to save and locate material without messaging and scrolling through everything."
workaround: Scrolling the full message history; screenshotting documents into the camera roll as a personal archive.

who: People paid biweekly (26 checks a year) trying to use monthly-cycle budgeting apps
what_breaks: Budget tools assume a calendar-month cycle, so biweekly earners maintain a parallel spreadsheet to map paychecks onto months.
quote: I’ve used a couple budgeting apps but they were based on monthly budgets while I get paid bu-weekly. So I always had to rely on my spreadsheets to make them work.
volume_evidence: 20 of 500 sampled recent YNAB reviews reference spreadsheets; 21 of 500 Goodbudget reviews and 13 of 250 Copilot reviews do the same — the spreadsheet is the consistent fallback across every budgeting app sampled.
workaround: Maintaining multiple spreadsheets alongside the app to reconcile paycheck timing with monthly categories.

who: Sole proprietors and 1099 workers using a consumer budgeting app as their books
what_breaks: There is no filtered or date-ranged export, so at tax time the user dumps their entire transaction history to a spreadsheet and filters it there to get a single category's year-to-date total.
quote: I have to export ALL my transactions, dating back to when I first started using the app, to a spreadsheet, then filter my searches there.
volume_evidence: Copilot has ~30,200 US ratings; 13 of 250 sampled recent reviews mention spreadsheets/Excel, most in a tax or business context. A Keeper user (2025-02-05) reports the same end state: "now I’m literally adding up all my expenses separately by category since bookkeeping it’s pretty expensive".
workaround: Full CSV export into Excel/Sheets and manual filtering and summing by Schedule C category.

who: Self-employed people who owe state self-employment tax in several states at once
what_breaks: No consumer tax tool models multi-state SE income, so the filer researches each state's rules by hand and computes quarterlies in a spreadsheet.
quote: I have to pay SE taxes in 4 states. Before FlyFin, I struggled with spreadsheets, spending hours researching specific tax policies
volume_evidence: FlyFin has only ~550 US ratings but 8 of 233 sampled reviews cite spreadsheets as the prior system; Keeper reviews show the same pattern ("I had to teach myself Excel to track my expenses which took a lot of time", 2024-02-21).
workaround: Per-state spreadsheets plus hours of manual research on each state's policy, or an expensive local CPA who miscalculates.

who: Extended families and friend groups on a shared trip who pool money up front and then split only what exceeds the pot
what_breaks: Expense-splitting apps model only per-expense splits, so a group with a common kitty has no way to record the pot and gets a settle-up number with no itemized backing.
quote: a pool of money to use up first, then we wanted to split anything beyond that pool of funds. The app doesn’t handle that situation
volume_evidence: Splitwise has ~27,800 US ratings and has fallen to a 3.98 average; 21 of 400 sampled recent reviews explicitly name a spreadsheet as the alternative.
workaround: Viewing raw activity history and redoing the math by hand: "The only option really is to view the 'activity' history and manually do the math to get to these numbers."

who: Friend groups logging a weekend trip's expenses on a free expense-splitting tier
what_breaks: A four-expenses-per-day cap turns a single weekend's costs into a week-long data-entry chore across several people, so groups abandon the app mid-trip.
quote: It’s now taking a week for my friends and I to add the expenses from one weekend trip! We’ve gone back to using a spreadsheet.
volume_evidence: Multiple independent 1-star reviews in the same sampled window say the same thing ("Don’t waste your time, just make a spreadsheet and do the math yourself", 2026-07-21; "Just use a spreadsheet, it’ll be cheaper and easier than this app", 2026-05-15); 21 of 400 sampled reviews name spreadsheets.
workaround: Reverting to a shared Google Sheet for the whole trip and settling manually over Venmo.

who: Families who adopted a shared-calendar app and later need to move to a different system or device
what_breaks: The shared calendar imports other calendars but has no export, so a household migrating to a wall display or Google Calendar re-types months of events by hand.
quote: I cannot export this calendar into anything else. It will import plenty of calendars, but everything in time tree stays in time tree.
volume_evidence: TimeTree has ~91,100 US ratings; 12 of 350 sampled recent reviews raise export or sync. A separate reviewer is stuck for the same reason: "his entire company uses it just because it’s difficult to transfer data out of it." (2025-12-05)
workaround: Manually re-entering every event into the destination calendar before deleting the app.

who: Working parents running a household with an au pair or split custody schedule alongside a work calendar
what_breaks: The family organizer is a walled garden with no two-way sync and no shareable calendar URL, so every appointment gets entered twice — once for work, once for the family.
quote: Doesn’t two-way sync with your other calendars so you have to manually update everything
volume_evidence: FamilyWall has ~23,100 US ratings; 29 of 500 sampled recent reviews mention sync or manual duplication. A Skylight owner reports the same double-entry problem after email forwarding silently broke (2026-07-30).
workaround: Entering every event in two places (work Outlook/Gmail and the family app) and manually keeping them aligned.

who: Households trying to eat healthier who cook from recipes found online
what_breaks: Recipes live on the open web with no structured nutrition or ingredient data, so people print them into a binder and hand-write the grocery list every week.
quote: we had to manually write down the grocery list of the items we needed and then whenever we were ready to actually cook it we’d have to go find the recipe again
volume_evidence: Mealime has ~54,000 US ratings and is being discontinued as of Sept 2026 ("I wish it wasn’t being discontinued!", 2026-09-10), pushing this population back to the manual workflow; AnyList reviewers describe the same fallback ("I’m just copying my recipes by hand or into Notion", 2026-06-06).
workaround: Printing recipes, hole-punching them into a binder, and hand-writing the shopping list before each store trip.
